claims.text: Previously studied type-A superconducting HEAs commonly contain large amounts of Nb and Ta and typically less than 20 at.% Ti.
The proposed starting alloy is a NbTi-based HEA with a dominant Nb-Ta matrix and less than 20 at.% Ti.
The starting alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
An HEA contains at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
Ti concentration will be increased while the relative fractions of the other principal elements are held constant.
Identical milling and sintering conditions will ensure phase homogeneity and comparable microstructural features across compositions.
Increasing Ti concentration lowers the alloy's overall valence electron count.
Increasing Ti concentration increases local lattice disorder.
Lowering VEC can increase the density of states at the Fermi level in the proposed NbTi-based HEA.
An increased density of states at the Fermi level strengthens electron-phonon coupling and thereby enhances superconductivity.
Ti-induced disorder modifies scattering processes that affect Tc and Hc2.
Tc in HEA superconductors exhibits systematic dependence on VEC, with trends that can differ from classical and amorphous alloys.
Binary Nb-Ti alloys have better superconducting properties than binary Nb-Ta alloys.
Ti-rich ternary Nb-Ti-Hf and Nb-Ti-Ta alloys and quaternary Nb-Ti-Ta-Hf alloys have shown the highest Hc2 values within their respective series.
Relative to the low-Ti baseline, a Ti-enriched NbTi-based HEA will have a higher superconducting transition temperature.
Relative to the low-Ti baseline, a Ti-enriched NbTi-based HEA may have a higher upper critical field.
The predicted enhancement applies only while the material remains a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Phase segregation or intermetallic formation can alter or mask the proposed superconducting trend.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that phase separation or intermetallic formation places the material outside the domain in which the prediction applies, whereas the falsification rule treats occurrence of those out-of-domain conditions as falsification.

The predicted outcome makes increased Hc2 only a possibility, but the falsification rule requires correlated increases in both Tc and Hc2; unchanged Hc2 could therefore be labeled falsifying even though it is compatible with the stated prediction.
